PALMER Department of Geophysics, The University of Western Ontario, London, Ontario Received April 13, 1970 Accepted for publication August 12, 1970 Paleomagnetic results from the Lake Superior region appear to indicate that Middle Keweenawan formations or magnetic divisions within formations can be correlated on the basis of magnetic polarity. The Logan sills, the volcanics of the Osler Group, the lava section at Alona Bay, the lower 6000 ft (1829 m) of North Shore volcanics, the lower 1000 ft (305 m) of Cape Gargantua volcanics and the lower 3000 ft (914 m) at Mamainse Point are of reverse polarity. Normal directions of magnetization, which differ from the reverse direc- tions of magnetization by amounts ranging from 140" to 163" occur throughout the Michipico- ten Island section, and in the upper p

nd Mamainse Point sections. Provided part of the section at Mamainse Point has been repeated by faulting, these new results, together with data from the literature, are compatible with a single polarity reversal in Middle Keweenawan time separating older reverse polarity rocks from stratigraph- ically younger normal polarity rocks. It is believed that this mean direction reflects a secondary component of magnetiza- tion which cannot be preferentially removed by alternating field demagnetization and which has caused the non anti-parallel alignment of normal and reverse populations of magnetization. An estimate of the pole position during Middle Keweenawan time can, however, be made by calculating a pole given equal weight to the mean normal and mean reverse pole. This is calculated to be 159" W, 42" N. f remanent magnetization were used to corre- late the various Keweenawan sequences around Lake Superior. The Logan sills, the volcanics of the Osler Group, the lava section at Alona Bay, the lower 6000 ft (1829 m) of North Shore volcanics, the lower 1000 ft (305 m) of Cape Gargantua volcanics and the lower 3000 ft (914 m) at Mamainse Point are of reverse polarity. Normal directions of magnetization, which differ from the reverse direc- tions of magnetization by amounts ranging from 140" to 163" occur throughout the Michipico- ten Island section, and in the upper p

nd Mamainse Point sections. Provided part of the section at Mamainse Point has been repeated by faulting, these new results, together with data from the literature, are compatible with a single polarity reversal in Middle Keweenawan time separating older reverse polarity rocks from stratigraph- ically younger normal polarity rocks. The mean direction of magnetization from a conglomer- ate test is defined with higher precision than would be expected from a randomly distributed population. It is believed that this mean direction reflects a secondary component of magnetiza- tion which cannot be preferentially removed by alternating field demagnetization and which has caused the non anti-parallel alignment of normal and reverse populations of magnetization. An estimate of the pole position during Middle Keweenawan time can, however, be made by calculating a pole given equal weight to the mean normal and mean reverse pole. This is calculated to be 159" W, 42" N. Introduction The paleomagnetic survey of the Keweena- wan rocks in the Lake Superior region by Dubois ( 1962) illustrated the potential of the paleomagnetic method in supplementing radio- metric dating for the purpose of effecting stratigraphic correlations in unfossiliferous rocks. Both remanent magnetic polarity and the

f remanent magnetization were used to corre- late the various Keweenawan sequences around Lake Superior. Some of the Middle Keweena- wan volcanic units examined by Dubois (1962), exhibited reverse (positive) magnetic polarity, whereas other units consisted entirely of nor- mal (negative) polarity, but it was only for the Logan sills and dikes that Dubois (1962) had evidence suggesting the age relations be- tween these two sets of magnetic directions. The efforts of the present study were con- centrated on the volcanic sequences which are generally assigned to the Middle Keweenawan (Halls 1966, p. 5). Some of these have not been sampled by previous investigators, while others, such as that at Mamainse Point, have only been partly studied (Dubois 1962). The purpose of this study, therefore, is to obtain a more comprehensive sample of the Keweena- wan volcanic sequences, in order to discover if the age relations between normal and reverse populations of magnetization, suggested by the earlier results from the Logan sills and dikes, are generally applicable to the Middle Ke- weenawan as a whole. Introduction The paleomagnetic survey of the Keweena- wan rocks in the Lake Superior region by Dubois ( 1962) illustrated the potential of the paleomagnetic method in supplementing radio- metric dating for the purpose of effecting stratigraphic correlations in unfossiliferous rocks. Both remanent magnetic polarity and the

f remanent magnetization were used to corre- late the various Keweenawan sequences around Lake Superior. Some of the Middle Keweena- wan volcanic units examined by Dubois (1962), exhibited reverse (positive) magnetic polarity, whereas other units consisted entirely of nor- mal (negative) polarity, but it was only for the Logan sills and dikes that Dubois (1962) had evidence suggesting the age relations be- tween these two sets of magnetic directions. The efforts of the present study were con- centrated on the volcanic sequences which are generally assigned to the Middle Keweenawan (Halls 1966, p. 5). Some of these have not been sampled by previous investigators, while others, such as that at Mamainse Point, have only been partly studied (Dubois 1962). The Logan sills, the volcanics of the Osler Group, the lava section at Alona Bay, the lower 6000 ft (1829 m) of North Shore volcanics, the lower 1000 ft (305 m) of Cape Gargantua volcanics and the lower 3000 ft (914 m) at Mamainse Point are of reverse polarity. Normal directions of magnetization, which differ from the reverse direc- tions of magnetization by amounts ranging from 140" to 163" occur throughout the Michipico- ten Island section, and in the upper p

nd Mamainse Point sections. Provided part of the section at Mamainse Point has been repeated by faulting, these new results, together with data from the literature, are compatible with a single polarity reversal in Middle Keweenawan time separating older reverse polarity rocks from stratigraph- ically younger normal polarity rocks. The mean direction of magnetization from a conglomer- ate test is defined with higher precision than would be expected from a randomly distributed population. It is believed that this mean direction reflects a secondary component of magnetiza- tion which cannot be preferentially removed by alternating field demagnetization and which has caused the non anti-parallel alignment of normal and reverse populations of magnetization. An estimate of the pole position during Middle Keweenawan time can, however, be made by calculating a pole given equal weight to the mean normal and mean reverse pole. This is calculated to be 159" W, 42" N. Introduction The paleomagnetic survey of the Keweena- wan rocks in the Lake Superior region by Dubois ( 1962) illustrated the potential of the paleomagnetic method in supplementing radio- metric dating for the purpose of effecting stratigraphic correlations in unfossiliferous rocks. Both remanent magnetic polarity and the

f remanent magnetization were used to corre- late the various Keweenawan sequences around Lake Superior. Some of the Middle Keweena- wan volcanic units examined by Dubois (1962), exhibited reverse (positive) magnetic polarity, whereas other units consisted entirely of nor- mal (negative) polarity, but it was only for the Logan sills and dikes that Dubois (1962) had evidence suggesting the age relations be- tween these two sets of magnetic directions. The efforts of the present study were con- centrated on the volcanic sequences which are generally assigned to the Middle Keweenawan (Halls 1966, p. 5). Some of these have not been sampled by previous investigators, while others, such as that at Mamainse Point, have only been partly studied (Dubois 1962). When the common bias was applied to each random direction in the ratio 1: 1, R ranged between 44.0 and 53.0. When the common bias was applied to each random direction in the ratio 1 :2, the values of R ranged between 13.9 and 30.8. In the trials where the common direction was given a weight of 1 while the random direction was given a weight of 3, the values of R ranged between 8.5 and 22.8. The value of R in the Mamainse Point and Copper Harbor conglomerate tests combined is 23.35 (Table VII). This value falls within the range which is produced when a secondary component in a specified direction, equal in magnitude to 50% of the original, is superimposed on the original direction. The results from the stability test experi- ments are taken to indicate that a secondary component of magnetization is present in these rocks which cannot be successfully removed by AC demagnetization, which predates at least in large part, the folding, and which is sufficient in magnitude to create the observed asymmetry between normal and reversed pop- ulations of magnetization. PALMER Department of Geophysics, The University of Western Ontario, London, Ontario Received April 13, 1970 Accepted for publication August 12, 1970 Paleomagnetic results from the Lake Superior region appear to indicate that Middle Keweenawan formations or magnetic divisions within formations can be correlated on the basis of magnetic polarity. The Logan sills, the volcanics of the Osler Group, the lava section at Alona Bay, the lower 6000 ft (1829 m) of North Shore volcanics, the lower 1000 ft (305 m) of Cape Gargantua volcanics and the lower 3000 ft (914 m) at Mamainse Point are of reverse polarity. Normal directions of magnetization, which differ from the reverse direc- tions of magnetization by amounts ranging from 140" to 163" occur throughout the Michipico- ten Island section, and in the upper p

nd Mamainse Point sections. Provided part of the section at Mamainse Point has been repeated by faulting, these new results, together with data from the literature, are compatible with a single polarity reversal in Middle Keweenawan time separating older reverse polarity rocks from stratigraph- ically younger normal polarity rocks. The mean direction of magnetization from a conglomer- ate test is defined with higher precision than would be expected from a randomly distributed population. It is believed that this mean direction reflects a secondary component of magnetiza- tion which cannot be preferentially removed by alternating field demagnetization and which has caused the non anti-parallel alignment of normal and reverse populations of magnetization. An estimate of the pole position during Middle Keweenawan time can, however, be made by calculating a pole given equal weight to the mean normal and mean reverse pole. This is calculated to be 159" W, 42" N. directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: Gif-sur-Yvette cedex, France b Estacion Volcanologica de Canarias, CSIC, La Laguna, Tenerife, Spain Received 6 June 1998; revised version received 20 November 1998; accepted 24 November 1998 Abstract We have sampled a sequence of 69 ¯ows in the island of El Hierro (Canary Islands). 46 of them belong to the El Golfo formation and 23 to the most recent rift formation. Radiometric dating brackets this section between 442 ka and 134 ka with six intermediate datings. All the samples were stepwise demagnetized, partly with alternative ®eld, partly thermally with very similar results. The large majority of the samples are characterized by a single stable component of magnetization. ChRM isolated after the ®rst steps of demagnetization are all of normal polarity. Inclinations are on average shallower than expected from a geocentered dipole ®eld, but consistent with results from other areas at the same latitude. Mean declinations of the rift and El Golfo sequences are both easterly deviated (about 5ë and 15ë respectively) and signi®cantly different suggesting that the section has undergone a progressive clockwise rotation. VGP scatter and directional scatter calculated for the rift sequence are consistent with available data from other geographical areas, and also with recent models of paleosecular vari

tle studied from a paleomag- netic point of view. Early studies [3±7] were aimed toward understanding of tectonic evolution of the is- lands, rather than documenting the paleosecular vari- ation. Consequently, of the over 350 data obtained from the Canary Island and Madeira, very few have been included in the data base used by Johnson and Constable [8] for the study of paleosecular variation. The most recent paleomagnetic studies in the Canary Islands have addressed the study of the Matuyama± Brunhes transition and the associated changes in the ®eld intensity [9], not speci®cally paleosecular variation. Recently, a combined K=Ar and magnetic polarity study of the Island of El Hierro [10], aiming for a better understanding of the island evolution, has also identi®ed a Brunhes epoch volcanic sequence which appeared suitable for a paleosecular variation study with reliable age control. This provided the opportunity to obtain modern data from this rather poorly explored region. 2. he most recent event. Like many other volcanic islands, El Hierro is formed by the competition of consecutive constructive and destruc- tive processes. Two main structural units succeeded in time: The oldest El TinÄor volcano was active dur- ing the upper part of the Matuyama Chron (between around 1.12 and 0.88 Ma) whereas the El Golfo edi®ce formed during the Brunhes period (between around 545 and 176 ka) [10]. The growth of instabil- Fig. 1. Schematic map of El Hierro island indicating the location of the El Golfo section. ities due to consecutive eruptions, perhaps coupled with magmatic overpressuring and pore ¯uid pres- surization during dyke emplacements [14], has led to a number of volcano ¯ank failures and conse- quent giant landslides with volumes of up to 1000 km 3 [15±17]. During the youngest part of the Brun- hes chron, a renewal of volcanic activity occurred through a well developed triple rift system building on top of the previous volcanic edi®ces of El TinÄor and El Golfo. Finally, the subsequent erosion of the landslides scars has resulted in the typical trilobate form of this island with its characteristic `Mercedes star' rift system [17] associated with topological ridges at angles of 120ë (oriented in NW, NE and S) and large embayments especially in the south-west

that for both the rift sequence and the El Golfo sequence below 261 ka, ®ltering does not drastically affect the characteristics of the record obtained from un®ltered data. For in- stance, the average paleomagnetic directions for the two sequences before and after ®ltering differ by only 2.7ë (rift sequence) and 1.2ë (El Golfo). On the other hand, ®ltering has a rather strong effect in the interval 261 to 158 ka: the three trachytic ¯ows and the three basaltic ¯ows are grouped in two directional clusters, and it is not possible to infer a realistic age interpolation for them. For this reason, we have decided not to consider these ¯ows in the discussion of the results. Our analysis is restricted to the rift sequence and to the El Golfo sequence below 261 ka. 4.2. This char- acteristics of the ®eld has been observed in many previous studies from geographically widespread sites (Wilson's off-centered dipole effect, see John- son and Constable [8] for references). tle studied from a paleomag- netic point of view. Early studies [3±7] were aimed toward understanding of tectonic evolution of the is- lands, rather than documenting the paleosecular vari- ation. Discussion Eleven of the 14 sites sampled were con- sidered to have reliable mean-site remanence directions. The strike and dip of the diabase sheet at the 11 sites (Table I) were obtained from information compiled by Thomson ( 1960, pp. 18-20; 1961a, pp. 46-47; 1961b, pp. 17, 19, 22, 24, 52; 1961c, p. 43). All tectonic corrections were made by simple rotation of the dip plane to the horizontal about the strike. Applying the fold test (Graham 1949) to all 11 mean site remanence directions, the values of a95 before and after tectonic correction were 5.4' and 8.6" respectively. Snedecor's F-ratio test for the null hypothesis (Larochelle 1968) indicates that there is a probability of 0.97 that the scatter in the remanence directions caused by applying tectonic corrections is significant. These tests show that the diabase acquired its remanence after solidification of the primary basin and arch structure. There is some evidence that Thomson's (1957) suggestion that post-solidification tec- degrees. tonics accentuated the basin and arch structure is correct. The

post-solidification NW- SE contraction approximately perpendicular to the basin axis (N 50°E) and parallel to the major NW-SE fault set. Unfortunately 3 of the 4 sites (5, 6, 7, and 8) collected to define the limbs of the Kerr Lake Arch which might have provided useful additional data, are not reliable. Thus the data favor a minor amount of secondary folding but not on a statistical significance basis. Sites 9 and 10 are adjacent to the Beaver and Kerr Lake faults respectively where the diabase sheet dips at 60' and 15" respectively. Application of tectonic corrections causes the remanence directions to scatter from consistent primary directions to completely inconsistent directions. This result suggests that the diabase SYMONS: PAL was not folded by more than a very few de- grees adjacent to the major faults contrary to Knight's ( 1922) suggestion. Sites 11 to 14 are collected on a N-S traverse perpendicular to the E-W ore vein structures of the Silverfields mine where the diabase sheet is flat-lying (Moore 1967; Petruk 1968). If post-solidification tectonics caused the sheet to fracture into blocks defined by the veins, then the remanence directions might reflect some consistent deformation pattern. SYMONS Geological Survey of Canada, 601 Booth Street, Ottawa, Canada Received September 9, 1969 Accepted for publication November 12, 1969 At Cobalt the Nipissing diabase intrusive occurs as a 1000 ft (-305 m) thick undulating sheet exposed in a series of basin and arch structures from which 112 specimens were collected at 14 sites. Paleomag- netic analysis of the cleaned natural remanence directions from the 11 acceptable sites suggests that these structures are dominantly primary. Minor post-solidification compression associated with the NW-SE trending faults may have amplified the primary NE-SW axial trends of the structures. Significant folding adjacent to the faults does not appear probable. The origin of the narrow argentiferous veins is probably related to minor local differential movements of large blocks of diabase or to cooling- contraction of the sheet. A revised pole position of 91.9 "E, 19.4 "N (dp = 3.9"; dm = 6.5") is given for the 2140 m.y. old

at 2180 2 40 m.y. by the RbSr whole rock method (Van Schmus 1965) and at 2095 m.y. by the K-A whole rock method (Lowdon et al. 1963). Miller ( 19 10) considered the diabase structure to be primary (i.e. to be formed prior to solidification of the diabase) except for nearly vertical fault offsets. Knight ( 1922) pointed to the gentle dips in the Cobalt Group and concluded that post-solidification folding of the diabase was at most very minor except adjacent to the major NE and NW trending faults. Thomson ( 1957) considered the basin and arch structure to be dominantlv ~rimarv .' The results of the palaeomagnetic studies of the Plio-Pleistocene basalts, middle Miocene andesites, and lower Cretaceous volcanic rocks, collected from the sites drawn in Fig. 1, are presented. Palaeomagnetic investigations of volcanic rocks of similar age in the countries surrounding Hungary were carried on by the following authors: BUCHA and others, NAIRN, in Slovakia, (BuCHA and others [114)), NAIRN [13, 14]), MIKHAYLOVA and GLEVASSKAYA, in Soviet-Transcarpathians (MIK~AYLOVA and GLEVASSKAYA [12]), COSTA-FORU (with co-workers), in Roumania (CosTA-For~u and others [2]). Methods The method of sampling and measuring adopted was similar to the one used com- monly. From a single outcrop if the conditions allowed at least six samples were collected. Out of each sample two cubes with an edge of 2.5 cms were cut. Beyond the natural remanent magnetization, the induced magnetization in the earth's mag- netic fieId was also measured. Throughout a sample group the Koenigsberger ratio Q, was i

up to 0.06 7/scale division. As a routine technique each sample is subjected to progressive demagnetization in alternating fields of up to several hundreds of oersteds in steps of 100 oersteds, the magnetization being determined after each step. Introduction The aim of the paper is to give an outline of palaeomagnetic investigations in Hungary. The results of the palaeomagnetic studies of the Plio-Pleistocene basalts, middle Miocene andesites, and lower Cretaceous volcanic rocks, collected from the sites drawn in Fig. 1, are presented. If the water went from carbonate rocks through volcanic rocks and back into carbonate rocks, it could, through ion exchange, lose calcium and magnesium dissolved from its first host and gain sodium. CONTENTS Introduction 57 Samples 58 Measurements and demagnetization 59 Discussion 61 Introduction Basic dike rocks are abundant and well ex- posed in the region of the Aland (Ahvenanmaa) archipelago. According to Sederholm (1890, 1934) the following sequence of dikes can be observed: 1) well preserved olivine diabase (dolerite) on the islands of Market and Sankan in the Aland Sea and near the shore of Eckerö. The rock is the youngest of the intrusive dikes in the region and certainly younger than rapakivi granite because it is found as dikes penetrating it (Fig. 1). 2) coarse grained, plagioclase rich (ossipite) diabase in the region outside the rapakivi gra- nite area. According to Frosterus (1892), these dikes are younger than rapakivi, but Sederholm (1934) and Hausen (1964) consider them to be somewhat older than rapakivi granite and associated granophyric dikes. The greatest num- ber of these dikes is encontered in an area SE of Föglö and in the SW part of Eckerö (Fig. 1). 8 13902—68 58 K. J. Groeber (1933) attributed the origin of these basaltic flows to eruptions following the second Andean tectonic phase during the Miocene. This age has been substantiated by the presence of Santa-Crucean fossils in tuffs contemporaneous with flows. Basalt I1 (Coyocholitense) is supposed to be of Upper Pliocene age, corres- ponding to effusions which followed the third Andean tectonic phase. In the zone outside the cordillera, this basalt forms extensive tablelands which are cut by the erosion of streams because it was later strongly uplifted. It is often possible to recognize the skeletal remains of the volcanoes from which these flows were extruded. Towards the end of the Pliocene, diastrophism produced a topography similar to the present one on which the products of a new effusive cycle accumulated in the Middle Pleistocene. Groeber (1933) named these flows Basalt I11 (Lower Chapuali- tense). They are highly eroded and generally exist singly, rarely forming successions of flows. The original volcanoes are well preserved. Valencio (Received 1969 July 3) Summary Results are presented of a study of 234 samples of Cenozoic basalts from the extra-Andean region of the Provinces of Mendoza and Neuquh in the Argentine Republic, between latitudes 34" S and 40" S. Valencio (Received 1969 July 3) Summary Results are presented of a study of 234 samples of Cenozoic basalts from the extra-Andean region of the Provinces of Mendoza and Neuquh in the Argentine Republic, between latitudes 34" S and 40" S. These basalts have been divided into seven groups of flows on the basis of their stratigraphy, ranging in age from the Miocene (Basalts I) to historic (Basalts VII). The TRM of Basalts V, VI and VII is normally polarized and it is concluded that they belong to the Brunhes geomagnetic epoch. The TRM directions of Basalt IV flows are neither parallel nor antiparallel to the axial dipole field. These differences in direction are significant and persistent after cleaning. It is therefore suggested that Basalt IV was extruded during a magnetic transition after the Brunhes geomagnetic epoch. Some Basalt I11 flows are normally polarized, some are reversely poled and some are magnetized obliquely to the axial dipole field. Hence the time of extrusion of these flows may span the Jaramillo and/or Olduvai events within the Matuyama epoch. Because the magnetic particles in redbeds usually have a high coercive force (> 1000 gauss), the most suitable labora- tory method for investigating the stability of the NRM is progressive thermal demagnetiza- tion. Thus, in highly serpentinized peridotires (serpentinites), most of the CRM is destroyed and the NRM becomes mainly viscous reinanent magnetization, rendering these rocks unsuitable for palcomagnetic work. On the other hand, in partially serpentinized peridotires, pyroxenites, and dunires, the CRM is highly stable and palcomagnetically reliable. A study of the stable directions of magnetization indicates that the Red Mountain ultramarie body was emplaced and serpentinized prior to the folding of the Franciscan formation. The stability of magneti- zation and removal of viscous components were verified by the results of a storage test and alternating-field demagnetization experiments, by the divergence of the mean directions of magnetization from that of the present field, and, most important, by the convergence of the directions after tilt correction. Palcomagnetic pole positions calculated from the mean directions suggest that the magnetic pole rapidly migrated southward into the Atlantic Ocean during late Mesozoic, possibly more than once, as proposed previously by Gromm and Gluskoter. Thus, in highly serpentinized peridotires (serpentinites), most of the CRM is destroyed and the NRM becomes mainly viscous reinanent magnetization, rendering these rocks unsuitable for palcomagnetic work. On the other hand, in partially serpentinized peridotires, pyroxenites, and dunires, the CRM is highly stable and palcomagnetically reliable. A study of the stable directions of magnetization indicates that the Red Mountain ultramarie body was emplaced and serpentinized prior to the folding of the Franciscan formation. The stability of magneti- zation and removal of viscous components were verified by the results of a storage test and alternating-field demagnetization experiments, by the divergence of the mean directions of magnetization from that of the present field, and, most important, by the convergence of the directions after tilt correction. Palcomagnetic pole positions calculated from the mean directions suggest that the magnetic pole rapidly migrated southward into the Atlantic Ocean during late Mesozoic, possibly more than once, as proposed previously by Gromm and Gluskoter. section_candidates.excerpt: rpentinization. The stablilly of mag- netization decreases with serpentinization, owing to the growth of larger magnetic grains. Thus, in highly serpentinized peridotires (serpentinites), most of the CRM is destroyed and the NRM becomes mainly viscous reinanent magnetization, rendering these rocks unsuitable for palcomagnetic work. On the other hand, in partially serpentinized peridotires, pyroxenites, and dunires, the CRM is highly stable and palcomagnetically reliable. A study of the stable directions of magnetization indicates that the Red Mountain ultramarie body was emplaced and serpentinized prior to the folding of the Franciscan formation. The stability of magneti- zation and removal of viscous components were verified by the results of a storage test and alternating-field demagnetization experiments, by the divergence of the mean directions of magnetization from that of the present field, and, most important, by the convergence of the directions after tilt correction. Palcomagnetic pole positions calculated from the mean directions suggest that the magnetic pole rapidly migrated southward into the Atlantic Ocean during late Mesozoic, possibly more than once, as proposed previously by Gromm and Gluskoter. WENSINK Geological Institute, State University, Utrecht (The Netherlands') (Received July 2, 1968) (Resubmitted October 30, 1968) SUMMARY Oriented samples were collected for paleomagnetic research from red horizons of the Gondwana sediments at a few localities in central India. The specimens were subjected to both alternating-field and thermal demagnetization and were measured on astatic magnetometers. Usually a stable direction of magnetization was observed only after thermal treatment. The following results were obtained: (1) The Upper Permian Kamthi Beds reveal a mean direction of magneti- zation given by D = 79.4 °, I = +61.6 ° (pole position 21.05°S 50.4°W; dp= 2.8 ° and dm = 3.7°); (2) The Lower Triassic Mangli Beds have D = 100.1 °, I = +62.8 ° (pole position 7.3°S 55.7°W; dp

of magneti- zation given by D = 79.4 °, I = +61.6 ° (pole position 21.05°S 50.4°W; dp= 2.8 ° and dm = 3.7°); (2) The Lower Triassic Mangli Beds have D = 100.1 °, I = +62.8 ° (pole position 7.3°S 55.7°W; dp = 5.7 ° and dm = 7.3°); (3) The Upper Triassic Pachmarhi Beds have D = 117.2 °, I = +48.9 ° (pole position 10.15°N 49.9°W; dp = 4.0 ° and dm= 6.1 °). These results combined with earlier data indicate that the Indian sub- continent has made a sinistral rotation of about 90 ° during Upper Paleozoic through Mesozoic times, without a considerable meridional shift. INTRODUCTION The present study deals with the paleomagnetism of rock samples from the Indian Gondwana sediments, collected during a field trip in the winter season of 1966-1967. The Indian subcontinent is considered to have formed part of the Gondwana continents of the Southern Hemisphere, because of paleontological similarities. Paleomagnetic studies on the Upper Cretaceous to Lower Eocene plateau basalts of the Deccan traps (DEuTSCH et al., 1959) as well as on the Jurassic Rajmahal traps (CLEGG et al., 1958) and Sylhet traps (ATHAVALE et al., 1963) have demonstrated that during the Upper Mesozoic India was situated south of the equator. WENSINK Geological Institute, State University, Utrecht (The Netherlands') (Received July 2, 1968) (Resubmitted October 30, 1968) SUMMARY Oriented samples were collected for paleomagnetic research from red horizons of the Gondwana sediments at a few localities in central India. The specimens were subjected to both alternating-field and thermal demagnetization and were measured on astatic magnetometers. Usually a stable direction of magnetization was observed only after thermal treatment. The following results were obtained: (1) The Upper Permian Kamthi Beds reveal a mean direction of magneti- zation given by D = 79.4 °, I = +61.6 ° (pole position 21.05°S 50.4°W; dp= 2.8 ° and dm = 3.7°); (2) The Lower Triassic Mangli Beds have D = 100.1 °, I = +62.8 ° (pole position 7.3°S 55.7°W; dp

of magneti- zation given by D = 79.4 °, I = +61.6 ° (pole position 21.05°S 50.4°W; dp= 2.8 ° and dm = 3.7°); (2) The Lower Triassic Mangli Beds have D = 100.1 °, I = +62.8 ° (pole position 7.3°S 55.7°W; dp = 5.7 ° and dm = 7.3°); (3) The Upper Triassic Pachmarhi Beds have D = 117.2 °, I = +48.9 ° (pole position 10.15°N 49.9°W; dp = 4.0 ° and dm= 6.1 °). These results combined with earlier data indicate that the Indian sub- continent has made a sinistral rotation of about 90 ° during Upper Paleozoic through Mesozoic times, without a considerable meridional shift. INTRODUCTION The present study deals with the paleomagnetism of rock samples from the Indian Gondwana sediments, collected during a field trip in the winter season of 1966-1967. The Indian subcontinent is considered to have formed part of the Gondwana continents of the Southern Hemisphere, because of paleontological similarities. Paleomagnetic studies on the Upper Cretaceous to Lower Eocene plateau basalts of the Deccan traps (DEuTSCH et al., 1959) as well as on the Jurassic Rajmahal traps (CLEGG et al., 1958) and Sylhet traps (ATHAVALE et al., 1963) have demonstrated that during the Upper Mesozoic India was situated south of the equator. The specimens were subjected to both alternating-field and thermal demagnetization and were measured on astatic magnetometers. Usually a stable direction of magnetization was observed only after thermal treatment. The following results were obtained: (1) The Upper Permian Kamthi Beds reveal a mean direction of magneti- zation given by D = 79.4 °, I = +61.6 ° (pole position 21.05°S 50.4°W; dp= 2.8 ° and dm = 3.7°); (2) The Lower Triassic Mangli Beds have D = 100.1 °, I = +62.8 ° (pole position 7.3°S 55.7°W; dp

of magneti- zation given by D = 79.4 °, I = +61.6 ° (pole position 21.05°S 50.4°W; dp= 2.8 ° and dm = 3.7°); (2) The Lower Triassic Mangli Beds have D = 100.1 °, I = +62.8 ° (pole position 7.3°S 55.7°W; dp = 5.7 ° and dm = 7.3°); (3) The Upper Triassic Pachmarhi Beds have D = 117.2 °, I = +48.9 ° (pole position 10.15°N 49.9°W; dp = 4.0 ° and dm= 6.1 °). These results combined with earlier data indicate that the Indian sub- continent has made a sinistral rotation of about 90 ° during Upper Paleozoic through Mesozoic times, without a considerable meridional shift. INTRODUCTION The present study deals with the paleomagnetism of rock samples from the Indian Gondwana sediments, collected during a field trip in the winter season of 1966-1967. The Indian subcontinent is considered to have formed part of the Gondwana continents of the Southern Hemisphere, because of paleontological similarities. Paleomagnetic studies on the Upper Cretaceous to Lower Eocene plateau basalts of the Deccan traps (DEuTSCH et al., 1959) as well as on the Jurassic Rajmahal traps (CLEGG et al., 1958) and Sylhet traps (ATHAVALE et al., 1963) have demonstrated that during the Upper Mesozoic India was situated south of the equator. INTRODUCTION The present study deals with the paleomagnetism of rock samples from the Indian Gondwana sediments, collected during a field trip in the winter season of 1966-1967. The Indian subcontinent is considered to have formed part of the Gondwana continents of the Southern Hemisphere, because of paleontological similarities. Paleomagnetic studies on the Upper Cretaceous to Lower Eocene plateau basalts of the Deccan traps (DEuTSCH et al., 1959) as well as on the Jurassic Rajmahal traps (CLEGG et al., 1958) and Sylhet traps (ATHAVALE et al., 1963) have demonstrated that during the Upper Mesozoic India was situated south of the equator. hey are overlain by Late Precambrian sediments and volcanics of the Cuddapah and Vindhyan Systems. Rocks of a Lower Paleozoic age are not found on the Indian subcontinent. The next stratigraphical unit is formed by a continental series which starts with glacial boulder beds and their associated peri-glacial beds of the Late Car- boniferous glaciation. From that time onwards sedimentation continues through the greater part of the Mesozoic until the Lower Cretaceous. All these deposits are classified in the Gondwana System. The rocks of the Gondwana System, which are chiefly composed of sand- stones and shales, are almost entirely deposited in fresh water. Intercalations of coal measures occur; they are mainly found in the lower part of the system. The subdivision of the Gondwana System into two subsystems is based on the content of plants: the Lower Gondwana System is characterized by the Glossopteris flora; the younger Upper Gondwana System can be distinguished from it by a cycadaceous Ptilophyllum flora. The transition between the Lower and the Upper Gondwana Systems takes place in the Upper Triassic. Apart from the subdivision into two separate systems advocated both by PASCOE (1959) and by KRISHNAN (1960), another subdivision is given by WADIA (1953) viz., into t

e Glossopteris flora; the younger Upper Gondwana System can be distinguished from it by a cycadaceous Ptilophyllum flora. The transition between the Lower and the Upper Gondwana Systems takes place in the Upper Triassic. Apart from the subdivision into two separate systems advocated both by PASCOE (1959) and by KRISHNAN (1960), another subdivision is given by WADIA (1953) viz., into three systems. Wadia distinguishes the Lower, the Middle, and the Upper Gondwana Systems. These coincide with the Upper Carboniferous-Permian, the Triassic, and the Jurassic together with the Lower Cretaceous respectively. The Gondwana sediments are deposited in a number of basins. The local stratigraphies which have been drawn up for the individual basins do not facilitate the establishment of a stratigraphy that is representative for the whole Gondwana System. The preservation of the Gondwana sediments is largely a result of faulting subsequent to the deposition of the beds concerned. A vast area of the western and central parts of the Indian peninsula is covered by a series of plateau basalts-the Deccan traps-which have a thickness of at least 1,500 m. One has a southerly declination revealed by demagnetization. It is the direction considered to be original and is represented by the data summarized in Table I. The second group comprises rocks whose N.R.M. directions grouped close to the present geomagnetic field and which upon demagnetization proved to have a secondary component sufficiently hard so that it was essentially unaffected by the cleaning techniques employed. OUTLINE OF GEOLOGY a) Upper Carboniferous and Lower Permian of the Inner Sudetic Depression The Inner Sudetic Depression (or Basin) has an elongated synclinal form. It is bordered by crystalline massifs save only in the south-west where there is tectonic contact with the Permian to Mesozoic fill of the Hronov Graben. The south-east and north-west margins of the Depres­ sion are formed by the crystalline rocks of the Góry Orlickie, Góry By­ strzyckie and Kłodzko massifs, a

A Namurian C to lower Westphalian A age is generally accepted for the Biały Kamień Formation. The Biały Kamień Formation gradually passes upwards to the Zacier Formation. In north-eastern part of the Depression the age of the Żacler Formation (up to 900 m thick) is regarded as Westphalian A and B, while in the south-western part of the Depression it also includes Westphalian C. The lower part of the formation consists mainly of sandstones and silt­ stones with coal seams. In the upper part of the formation sandstones and conglomerates dominate. On the north-eastern flank of the Inner Sudetic Depression the Glinik Formation, 100—600 m thick, formerly known as the „Ottweiler Schich- ten”, is transgressive over the Żacler, and locally over the Wałbrzych Formation. It has a Westphalian C — Lower Stephanian age (Grochol­ ski, 1965) and with a succession of conglomerates and sandstones alternating with red siltstones is lithologically distinct from the under­ lying Żacler Formation. g upwards into kaolinitic shales and siderite- -bearing siltstones. According to Dziedzic (1966), deposition of the Nowa Ruda Formation began in the Lower Carboniferous. A Namurian C to lower Westphalian A age is generally accepted for the Biały Kamień Formation. The Biały Kamień Formation gradually passes upwards to the Zacier Formation. In north-eastern part of the Depression the age of the Żacler Formation (up to 900 m thick) is regarded as Westphalian A and B, while in the south-western part of the Depression it also includes Westphalian C. The lower part of the formation consists mainly of sandstones and silt­ stones with coal seams. In the upper part of the formation sandstones and conglomerates dominate. On the north-eastern flank of the Inner Sudetic Depression the Glinik Formation, 100—600 m thick, formerly known as the „Ottweiler Schich- ten”, is transgressive over the Żacler, and locally over the Wałbrzych Formation. ent paleomagnetic data must be considered as a maximum estimate of the paleomagnetic field secular variation. It might be argued that the formation of the Monteregian Hills may have been an event of short duration, so that the above data cannot be used as a reliable gage of the secular varia- tion in Cretaceous time. It is pointed out, how- ever, that the group of intrusives has witnessed at least one earth's field reversal during its c.ooling, and, if it is correct to estimate with Cox and Dalrymple [1967] that this phenome- non spreads over about 5000 years, the Monte- regian Hills may have taken that long to cool through the Curie point of magnetite. In the perspective of the numerous Rb/Sr and K/Ar age determinations reported by Fairbairn et al. [1963] ,on the Monteregian Hills, it appears, however, that the group of intrusives may in fact have taken several million years to form. That the earth's field was apparently entirely dipolar in Cretaceous time is also suggested by the apparently reliable pole positions derived from other widely separated North American formations of this period. The high clustering of these poles about their center of gravity [Larochelie, 1968a] suggests that the 'wobble' of the dipole at that time was much less pro- nounced t

supports the view that the Oka and Mount Megantic intrusives are true extensions of the Monteregian Hills proper. Finally, the low angular standard deviation of the analyzed data suggests that in Cretaceous time the non-dipole component of the earth's magnetic field was less important relative to the dipole field than it is today. Bandelier Tuff The Bandelier Tuff forms gently sloping plateaus that cover 500 square miles on the north, east, and west flanks of the Jemez Mountains. These plateaus are deeply dissected by radial streams, and numerous steep-walled canyons in the tuff provide excellent exposures for sampling and detailed stratigraphic studies. The formation consists of two major ash-flow members; each member is underlain by a genetically related, bedded air-fall pumice. The bedded air-fall pumice beneath the Otowi Member was named the Guaje Member by Griggs, but the air-fall pumice associated with the ash-flow tuff of the Tshirege Member was apparently included by him within the base of the Tshirege Member. In this paper we will follow the usage of Smith and Bailey (1966) and use the informal terms, lower member and upper member. The lower member comprises Grigg's Otowi (an ash-flow unit) and the underlying Guaje Member (the associated air-fall unit), and the upper member constitutes the Tshirege Member, including the basal air-fall pumice. Thus, each of the lower and upper members consist of an ash-flow unit and its associated basal air-fall pumice. The lower member overlies a marked erosional unconformity that is de- veloped on the older volcanic rocks of the Jemez Mountains. The upper member, in turn, is separated from the lower member by a marked erosional disconformity and locally by bedded tuffs, glowing avalanche deposits, and volcanic sediments that related to the Cerro Toledo Rhyolite of the Toledo Caldera (PL 1). The internal stratigraphy of both members of

es permit correlation of units within each member with a high degree of confidence. The phenocryst mineralogy of the Bandelier Tuff is at first glance monotonously simple: major quartz, sanidine, and minor clinopyroxene, fayalite, and oxides. However, preliminary studies (Smith and Bailey, 1966) show that in the upper member, and prob- ably also in the lower member, systematic chemical and mineralogical changes on January 18, 2014memoirs.gsapubs.orgDownloaded from 216 STUDIES IN VOLCANOLOGY are recorded in pumices from successively emplaced flows. In the upper mem- ber, the phenocryst content changes from about 5 percent in the basal air-fall pumice and lower ash flows to more than 30 percent in upper units. In the uppermost unit, anorthoclase and hypersthene take the place of sanidine and fayalite, and there is a marked decrease in quartz content. This upper anortho- clase unit is unique in the Jemez Mountains and is critical to the correlation of the Bandelier Tuff inside and outside the Valles Caldera. It is this unit that dominates the outcrop on the structural dome within the caldera, whereas only a few remnants have survived erosion outside the caldera. Intracaldera Rhyolites The rhyolites within the Valles Caldera may be conveniently divided into three group

ggests a temporal succession of the principal domes from Cerro del Medio westward to San Antonio Mountain, and, as will be discussed later in this paper, the K-Ar and paleomagnetic studies tend to confirm this general succession. Warm Springs dome, a small endogenous rhyolite dome that is now being exhumed from young lake beds and alluvium may belong to this subgroup, but its stratigraphic relationship with the other units is not cer- tainly known. The youngest rhyolite units in the Valles Caldera are the ash flows of Battleship Rock and the overlying obsidian flow of Banco Bonito, both of which apparently issued from the same vent. Petrographically, the rhyolites of Cerro del Medio are almost without phenocrysts, but an occasional small sanidine crystal may be seen. The other late rhyolite units, discussed here, contain phenocrysts of quartz, sanidine, biotite, and oxides, and show a general increase in femic minerals and total phenocryst content westward from Cerro del Medio. Hornblende and plagio- clase are common in the youngest, westernmost units (San Antonio Moun- tain, Battleship Rock, and Banco Bonito). PALEOMAGNETIC STUDIES Methods The experimental factors that control paleomagnetic reliability have been discussed in earlier papers (Cox and others, 1963; Doell and others, 1966). Briefly, the only practical criterion is to ascertain that the primary stable component of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) has been clearly identified and measured. This requires the collection of multiple samples from the igneous unit in question and the application of partial demagnetization techniques to remove the less stable secondary components of remanent magnetization that may have been imparted by the effects of lightning (Cox, 1961; Graham, 1961) or by long exposure in the earth's magnetic field (Rimbert, 1956). MEX. 219 Discussion of Paleomagnetic Results It is convenient to discuss the paleomagnetic studies in reverse stratigraphic order. The two youngest units studied, the obsidian flow of Banco Bonito (S47) and the welded tuff of Battleship Rock (S46), are both normally magnetized. Younger Volcanic Series Lavas of the Younger Volcanic Series flooded the much eroded stumps of the old volcano to form an extensive intramontane plain, which slopes away from a central ridge. Two major periods of eruption are recognized, thought to have been separated by a relatively short period of quiescence. The Early Lavas are now only exposed in southwest Mauritius (Fig. 2), but may well extend under the Late Lavas (Simpson, 1951). These Early Lavas are mas- sive to somewhat vesicular alkali olivine basalts, usually 3 to 10 m thick. Petrographically and chemically they form a rather uniform series and are nepheline normative (Walker and Nicolaysen, 1954). The Late Lavas cover the remainder of the island between the older massifs and were erupted from a chain of vents extending in a line striking north-northeast through Curepipe in the center of the isknd. The surface of the Late Lavas has been little modified by erosion, although a number of gorges have been cut by consequent streams. As recognized by all workers, the Late Lavas must be very young geologically. The lavas generally are thin (1 to 8 m) and highly vesicular, suggesting a rather volatile magma. They are entirely basal

The lavas generally are thin (1 to 8 m) and highly vesicular, suggesting a rather volatile magma. They are entirely basaltic and contain abundant olivine phenocrysts. Many of the lavas are relatively coarse grained, doleritic basalts with a subophitic or ophitic texture. Compositionally the Late Lavas show little variation and are nepheline normative; they are characterized by remarkably low potassium contents for alkali olivine basalts (Walker and Nicolaysen, 1954). Dating was undertaken by the K-Ar method mainly on whole rock samples that showed little or no alteration in thin sec- tion. The dating techniques used were de- scribed by McDougall (1964, 1966). Potassium was measured by flame photometry (Cooper, 1963), and the isotope dilution method was used for determining argon. A Reynolds-type mass spectrometer in the static mode of opera- tion was employed to measure the isotopic ratios of the argon. Younger Volcanic Series Lavas of the Younger Volcanic Series flooded the much eroded stumps of the old volcano to form an extensive intramontane plain, which slopes away from a central ridge. Two major periods of eruption are recognized, thought to have been separated by a relatively short period of quiescence. The Early Lavas are now only exposed in southwest Mauritius (Fig. 2), but may well extend under the Late Lavas (Simpson, 1951). These Early Lavas are mas- sive to somewhat vesicular alkali olivine basalts, usually 3 to 10 m thick. Petrographically and chemically they form a rather uniform series and are nepheline normative (Walker and Nicolaysen, 1954). The Late Lavas cover the remainder of the island between the older massifs and were erupted from a chain of vents extending in a line striking north-northeast through Curepipe in the center of the isknd. The surface of the Late Lavas has been little modified by erosion, although a number of gorges have been cut by consequent streams. As recognized by all workers, the Late Lavas must be very young geologically. The lavas generally are thin (1 to 8 m) and highly vesicular, suggesting a rather volatile magma. They are entirely basal

The lavas generally are thin (1 to 8 m) and highly vesicular, suggesting a rather volatile magma. They are entirely basaltic and contain abundant olivine phenocrysts. Many of the lavas are relatively coarse grained, doleritic basalts with a subophitic or ophitic texture. Compositionally the Late Lavas show little variation and are nepheline normative; they are characterized by remarkably low potassium contents for alkali olivine basalts (Walker and Nicolaysen, 1954). A Reynolds-type mass spectrometer in the static mode of opera- tion was employed to measure the isotopic ratios of the argon. The terms magnetically "hard" and "soft" are used here to describe the amount of N.R.M. intensity associated with low coercivities. A magnetically soft sample loses its intensity of magnetization relatively rapidly during a.f. demagnetization and is therefore potentially more unstable than a magnetically hard rock. Introduction One project of the Dominion Observatory has been to obtain a record of the Upper Paleo- zoic geomagnetic field, from paleomagnetic studies of sedimentary rock formations of Eastern Canada. In this paper, results from red sediments of the Cumberland Group in Nova Scotia are described. These and previous re- sults of this project are then summarized, and from this summary certain broad features of the geomagnetic field in Eastern Canada are apparent. Introduction A considerable number of paleomagnetic studies of North American Precambrian rock units have been reported in the literature. How- ever, the geological age of most of the units studied is presently known only within wide limits. The construction of a North American Precambrian polar wandering curve will require many more paleomagnetic results from rock units that have been radiometrically dated.
